title.en: Cost drivers: tokens, inference, GPU, storage, vector DB

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How tokens, inference behavior, GPU utilization, storage, and vector databases drive AI costs.
- 2) How workload characteristics (context length, batch size, quantization, index type, replication) affect cost and latency.
- 3) Practical levers to reduce spend without harming quality: prompt compression, caching, batching, quantization, right-sizing GPUs, and index tuning.

blocks.title: LLM Cost Optimization: Token Economics for Agentic FinOps
blocks.label: Course Video

objectiveBefore.fr: Pendant cette vidéo, repérez les éléments qui illustrent « What You Will Learn » avant de poursuivre.
objectiveBefore.en: While watching, identify the elements that illustrate “What You Will Learn” before continuing.

body.en:
Tokens: Most hosted LLMs price per 1K or 1M tokens, often with different rates for input vs output. Total token cost = input tokens × rate_in + output tokens × rate_out.

Long system prompts, unnecessary context, and high output caps inflate spend. Caching prompts and compressing context lower input tokens; constraining max output and using function/tool outputs reduce output tokens.

Inference: For self-hosted models, the dominant driver is GPU time per request. Throughput (tokens/s) depends on model size, precision (FP16 vs INT8/4), batch size, and KV-cache reuse.

Micro-batching increases utilization; quantization reduces memory bandwidth and can raise throughput with minor quality impact. GPU: Cloud GPU cost is billed per hour; effective cost per token drops as utilization rises.

Right-size memory to model needs (avoid overprovisioning), prefer reserved/savings plans or spot where appropriate, colocate model and data to minimize idle waits, and monitor p95 latency vs utilization to avoid over-batching. Storage: Object storage holds logs, prompts, and embeddings.

Costs come from GB-month, requests, and egress. Apply lifecycle policies (hot → warm → cold), compress text, and deduplicate embeddings.

Vector DB: Cost scales with number of vectors, dimensionality, index type, and replication. HNSW offers fast recall with higher memory; IVF/IVFPQ reduces memory with some recall trade-off.

Read/write mix matters: write-heavy workloads pay more for rebuild/compaction; read-heavy workloads pay for query CPU and memory. Tuning parameters (efSearch, nprobe), reducing dimensionality, and lowering replicas reduce spend.

• Token spend is driven by prompt length and output caps; reduce via prompt compression, RAG with minimal relevant context, and caching.
• Inference and GPU costs depend on throughput and utilization; micro-batching and quantization lower cost per token while maintaining latency targets.
• Storage and vector DB costs scale with vectors × dimensions × replicas and index parameters; tune for read/write mix and acceptable recall.

• Token volume is the primary driver for hosted LLMs; trim prompts and cap outputs.
• GPU time drives self-hosted inference cost; maximize utilization via batching and quantization.
• Vector DB and storage scale with dimensions, count, and replicas; tune indexes and lifecycle policies.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now identify major AI cost drivers and apply practical techniques to reduce spend without sacrificing outcomes.

title.en: Unit economics by user, request, workflow and outcome

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to define unit economics at the request, user, workflow, and outcome levels. 2) How to build cost formulas that include tokens, GPU time, vector queries, storage, and overheads. 3) How to allocate shared and fixed costs and link cost to business outcomes (cost per successful result).

Requests: Cost per request aggregates variable components: C_req = (tokens_in × rate_in) + (tokens_out × rate_out) + (GPU_seconds × $/sec) + (vector_queries × $/query) + (egress × $/GB) + orchestration overhead. Track p50/p95 cost and latency.

Users: Cost per user per period = sum of their request costs + allocated fixed costs (e.g., support, storage) attributable to that user. Segment by cohort (free vs paid) to reveal margin differences.

Workflows: Multi-step pipelines include embedding creation, retrieval, ranking, generation, and post-processing. Attribute cost to each step to find the highest-cost stages and optimize (e.g., cache embeddings, batch retrieval, reduce re-ranking calls).

Outcomes: Cost per successful outcome = average cost per attempt ÷ success rate. Tie definition of success to business goals (issue resolved, document drafted, lead qualified).

This reframes spending in terms of value delivered, not just activity. Fixed/Shared Costs: Amortize fine-tuning, model hosting, and reserved GPUs over time or usage.

Driver-based allocation (GPU-seconds, tokens processed, storage GB-month) aligns incentives better than flat splits. Measurement: Instrument token counts, GPU time, vector ops, and cache hit rates.

Use tagging to attribute costs to users/teams/workflows, and run sensitivity analyses (e.g., token caps, batch size, efSearch) to forecast unit cost changes.

body.en:
• C_request blends token, GPU, vector, and network/storage costs; track by percentile and by feature.
• Allocate fixed costs using driver-based metrics (GPU-seconds, tokens, GB-month) to keep usage and cost aligned.
• Cost per successful outcome connects spend to value via funnel metrics like acceptance or resolution rate.

• Define units clearly: per request, per user-period, per workflow stage, and per successful outcome.
• Use driver-based formulas to attribute both variable and fixed costs.
• Optimize the largest contributors first and measure impact on cost per success, not just cost per request.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now model unit economics across requests, users, workflows, and outcomes and tie spend to value.

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to forecast AI costs by separating pilot (POC) activity from production adoption and usage intensity
- 2) How to use funnel conversion, ramp curves, and leading indicators to build scenarios with confidence ranges
- 3) How to translate adoption forecasts into capacity (GPU/endpoint) and budget plans while managing risk

Pilots and production behave differently. Pilots (POCs) are short-lived, low-scale, high-variance experiments intended to validate feasibility and value.

Production adoption is longer-lived, stabilized, and governed by SLOs, compliance, and change controls. Effective forecasting separates: 1) volume (how many pilots enter the funnel, how many convert to production), 2) intensity (tokens/calls per user or per workflow; GPU-seconds per request), and 3) timing (ramp curves from launch to steady state).

A funnel-based approach models stages: discovery → pilot → limited production (canary) → full production. Each stage has a conversion rate and lead time.

Production ramps follow S-curves or phased rollouts (e.g., 5%/20%/50%/100%). Usage intensity shifts from exploratory (spiky, prompt-heavy) to operational (more consistent rates tied to business events).

Key drivers to capture: user counts, requests per user, token mix (prompt vs completion), concurrency, model choice (and cost per 1K tokens or per GPU-hour), caching/hybrid strategies, guardrails that affect re-tries, seasonality, and vendor rate limits. Forecast uncertainty with range assumptions (min/base/max) or probability distributions and use scenario or Monte Carlo simulation to produce P50/P90 cost bands.

Leading indicators improve accuracy: backlog of pilots, security reviews completed, API key requests, feature flags enabled, approval tickets, and early SLO metrics (latency/error rates) that gate rollouts. Translate forecasts into capacity needs (e.g., peak TPS, GPU-hours, endpoint autoscaling headroom), reserve or right-size capacity, and tie budgets to adoption milestones with stage gates to control spend risk.

• Funnel-based forecasting: Model pilot → production conversion rates and lead times to estimate when workloads go live
• Ramp curves and steady state: Use phased rollouts or S-curves for production usage growth and steady-state intensity
• Scenario ranges and leading indicators: Apply min/base/max (or Monte Carlo) and track signals like approvals, API keys, and early TPS to refine forecasts

• Separate pilots from production; use funnel conversion, lags, and ramp curves
• Forecast with ranges and leading indicators to produce P50/P90 budgets
• Translate adoption into capacity plans (TPS/GPU-hours) and staged budgets to manage risk
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to design a robust tagging and metadata taxonomy for AI workloads across clouds and vendors 2) How to allocate shared AI costs (GPU clusters, gateways, vector databases) fairly using usage-based drivers 3) How to enforce tagging, remediate untagged spend, and operationalize showback/chargeback

Cost allocation assigns spend to business owners using consistent dimensions. For AI, include: application/product, team/cost center, environment (dev/test/prod), workload type (training vs inference), model/provider, region, and data sensitivity.

Implement tags/labels on cloud resources (AWS tags, Azure tags, GCP labels) and propagate metadata through AI platforms (ML platforms, model registries, inference gateways) so each request or job carries project/team identifiers. Where vendors lack native tags (e.g., hosted LLM APIs), use per-project API keys or a proxy/gateway that injects headers and logs usage by owner.

Shared services (GPU clusters, feature stores, vector DBs, gateways) require allocation bases that reflect causal consumption: GPU-hours, tokens, requests, storage GB-months, read/write ops, or concurrency. Choose drivers that are measurable, auditable, and aligned with cost causality; consider floors/minimums for underutilization, and separate fixed vs variable components.

Establish showback (visibility without billing) before chargeback (internal billing) to drive behavior. Handle untagged or partially tagged spend with automated policies: required-tag enforcement at create time, policy-as-code, budget alerts, and periodic backfill using resource ancestry (projects/subscriptions/accounts), IAM ownership, or service logs.

Group costs with Cost Categories (AWS), Cost Allocation Rules (Azure), or Labels/Projects (GCP) to create business views. Maintain a controlled tag dictionary, validate values (e.g., via OPA/Tag Policies), and version changes.

Integrate allocation outputs with finance (GL/cost centers) and define unit economics (cost per 1K tokens, per request, per GPU-hour) to benchmark teams and models.

• Tagging taxonomy: Standardized keys for app/team/env/workload/model/region with governance and validation
• Allocation bases: Use causal drivers (GPU-hours, tokens, requests, storage) and separate fixed vs variable costs
• Showback vs chargeback: Start with transparency, then bill internally once data quality and buy-in are achieved

• Define and enforce a standardized tagging schema; propagate metadata through AI platforms
• Allocate shared costs with causal, auditable drivers and separate fixed vs variable components
• Use automation to remediate untagged spend and operationalize showback/chargeback
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.
